transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-03-11
Start: 21:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (NobleMed ML Eng), Ruth Gomez (NobleMed CTO), Alina Park (NobleMed Product), J. Lee (NobleMed Infra)

Summary: Hands-on Optimize console walkthrough focused on creating and evaluating INT8 and FP8 quantization profiles, tradeoffs between latency and answer quality for NobleMed's clinical summarization workload. Customer wants guidance on safe rollback/fallback rules and how to interpret quality regressions in evals.

Topics covered:
- Quick intro to Redwood Optimize and sandbox
- How Optimize proposes quantization profiles (INT8/FP8/mixed)
- Live demo: run profile sweep against 3 prompt sets (short clinical notes, multi-sentence discharge summaries, medication reconciliation)
- Interpreting evaluation metrics (BLEU-ish, embedding-similarity, human pass/fail)
- Fallback rules and canary rollouts
- Pricing/throughput implications for Hosted vs Dedicated

Transcript body:
[00:00] Avery Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. um we wanted to run a fairly pragmatic session today — kind of a hands-on walkthrough of Optimize with your workload in mind. diego and priya are here to run the sandbox demos.
[00:18] Ruth Gomez: hi thanks, yeah we had some internal debate — are we comfortable with int8 for summaries? our concern is hallucinations increasing.
[00:28] Diego Morales: great question. so the typical pattern is int8 gives a big cost cut with marginal latency change on some hardware, fp8 often keeps quality closer to fp16 at a slightly higher perf cost. but, um, results are model and prompt dependent.
[00:44] Priya Kapoor: also worth noting the console shows a per-prompt sensitivity heatmap — so you can see which prompts regress more under int8.
[00:55] Samir Patel: can you show that? we have three priority prompt types — short notes, mid-length discharge summaries, and the multi-turn med reconciliation flows.
[01:07] Diego Morales: yeah we'll import a small eval set now. i'm uploading the CSV — bear with me, network's a bit slow.
[01:26] (file upload noise)
[01:35] Diego Morales: ok file's in. starting a profile sweep: baseline fp16 -> int8 static -> int8 qprofile -> fp8 mixed. estimated run time ~ 8 minutes for 300 samples.
[01:51] Ruth Gomez: how does the sandbox map to production throughput? our SLA is 200 qps for summaries during day hours.
[02:02] Priya Kapoor: the sandbox uses one pod so latency is single-shard — it's not auto scaled. we'll show per-token latencies and then show how autoscaling and dedicated pools change that.
[02:18] Samir Patel: rough question — if fp8 looks fine, what's the cost delta vs fp16?
[02:25] Avery Chen: on our hosted offering fp8 is usually ~20-40% cheaper than fp16 depending on sequence length and batch. int8 can be 40-70% cheaper but again depends on quality constraints.
[02:40] Alina Park: are those numbers for CPU or GPU?
[02:43] Diego Morales: GPU — mixed precision kernels. for CPU it's not common for these model sizes.
[02:50] (crosstalk)
[03:10] Diego Morales: sweep started — first set is short clinical notes. console shows delta table now: latency median FP16 120ms, INT8 static 95ms, INT8 qprofile 100ms, FP8 110ms. quality metric (embedding sim against baseline) average: FP16 1.00, FP8 0.995, INT8 qprofile 0.97, INT8 static 0.92.
[03:38] Samir Patel: hmm that int8 static drop to 0.92 — that's concerning. what's typical for our instruction-following prompts?
[03:45] Priya Kapoor: static int8 is heavier — it doesn't adapt quant per-layer. qprofile is the middle ground — we recommend qprofile when you have heterogeneous prompt lengths.
[03:57] Ruth Gomez: can you show an example where int8 caused a factual error?
[04:04] Diego Morales: yeah pulling a failed sample: baseline says "patient has no known drug allergies" — int8 static produced "patient reports allergy to penicillin" — that's a polarity hallucination. you'll see it flagged in the regression list.
[04:20] Alina Park: yikes. how does rollback look? can we route a percent of traffic to fp16 automatically?
[04:27] Avery Chen: yes — console supports canary rollouts with automatic quality gates. you set thresholds (e.g., embedding similarity > 0.98, zero critical hallucinations flagged) and rollback triggers.
[04:39] Diego Morales: plus you can set rule-based fallbacks for sensitive prompt types — route med reconciliation prompts to fp16/FP8 while less sensitive ones go to int8.
[04:53] Samir Patel: that rule-based routing is key for us; a lot of our pipeline labels sensitivity at the prompt layer so that fits.
[05:05] (brief pause)
[05:22] Diego Morales: second sweep group: discharge summaries (mid-length). latency medians: FP16 220ms, FP8 195ms, INT8 qprofile 170ms, INT8 static 150ms. embedding sim: FP16 1.00, FP8 0.997, INT8 qprofile 0.985, INT8 static 0.95. human pass/fail lab: FP16 96% pass, FP8 94%, INT8 qprofile 90%, INT8 static 82%.
[05:54] Ruth Gomez: those human pass rates — how are they defined?
[06:00] Priya Kapoor: we provide an annotation UI; pass is defined by your eval criteria — typically factual accuracy, critical content present, no PII leakage. you can upload your own rubric.
[06:12] Alina Park: how representative is the sample? how many prompts to be confident?
[06:16] Diego Morales: rule of thumb is 1k diverse samples for production confidence; for pilot we do 200-500 to find obvious regressions.
[06:27] Samir Patel: ok we'll prepare 500.
[06:30] (timestamped note)
[06:40] Diego Morales: next, multi-turn reconciliation flows — interestingly, int8 qprofile had more token-level drift: context window interactions lead to higher error rates. FP8 preserved conversation state better.
[06:56] Ruth Gomez: so for multi-turn we should prefer FP8?
[06:58] Priya Kapoor: often yes, or mixed strategies: keep KV/cache in higher precision and quantize other weights. Redwood supports hybrid precision profiles.
[07:12] Avery Chen: i want to call out cost modeling: for your 200 qps SLA, switching to Dedicated with reserved capacity gives predictable per-hour costs and better tail-latency guarantees. Hosted is simpler but has variability at high spikes.
[07:28] J. Lee: what about encryption and KMS for private deployments? we need key control for PHI.
[07:33] Diego Morales: Private/VPC supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and audit logs. we can show the private deployment checklist in the follow-up doc.
[07:45] (crosstalk)
[08:00] Diego Morales: sweep finished. summary dashboard rendering now — showing per-prompt regression tags and a suggested rolling plan: start with qprofile at 5% traffic, run targeted human evals on flagged prompts, then escalate if no critical issues.
[08:19] Alina Park: what's the recommended monitoring cadence post-rollout?
[08:23] Priya Kapoor: continuous — metric drift alerts tied to embedding similarity, hallucination counts, and latency p90. we suggest daily for first week then weekly once stable.
[08:34] Samir Patel: can we integrate these alerts with PagerDuty/Slack?
[08:37] Diego Morales: yes — we support webhooks, PagerDuty, and CloudWatch/Stackdriver integrations.
[08:43] Ruth Gomez: curious — how do you measure hallucinations automatically?
[08:47] Priya Kapoor: combination of heuristics and reference-based checks; for closed-domain facts we can run entity-checkers, for open-ended we surface likely hallucinations via classifier and human review.
[09:00] (note: small overlap in speaker labeling here)
[09:15] Avery Chen: ok let's demo creating a rollout in console — creating a canary with 2 rules: (1) embedding sim > 0.985 across sample set, (2) zero critical hallucinations in last 1000 responses.
[09:32] (typing noise)
[09:40] Diego Morales: creating canary, attaching metric hooks. setting auto rollback to 10 minutes.
[09:50] Samir Patel: is there a throttling mechanism if an upstream spike happens?
[09:54] Priya Kapoor: yes traffic shaping, burst buffer, and graceful degradation to lower-capacity models or cached responses.
[10:05] Ruth Gomez: we also need to understand legal/audit implications; if model returns PHI by mistake, how are logs stored?
[10:13] Avery Chen: audit logs are encrypted and can be configured to mask PII; retention policies are configurable for compliance.
[10:20] J. Lee: any SOC2 or ISO certificates?
[10:23] Diego Morales: yes we provide SOC 2 Type II and are in-process with ISO 27001; we'll send the compliance pack.
[10:33] Ruth Gomez: good, please share.
[10:37] (brief pause)
[10:55] Diego Morales: quick note on fallback strategies — we recommend multi-tier fallback: (1) model variant fallback (fp8->fp16), (2) routing to Dedicated region, (3) static rule for sensitive prompts. we also keep a small cache of approved responses for extremely sensitive queries.
[11:18] Samir Patel: can we pin a particular model version?
[11:21] Priya Kapoor: yes model version pinning is supported and part of your rollout policy.
[11:26] Alina Park: what about batch size tuning? we tried batch=8 earlier and saw tail latency spikes.
[11:32] Diego Morales: batch sizing is workload-dependent—Optimize suggests batch heuristics based on sequence length distribution and latency SLOs. you can lock batch size per-route.
[11:42] (crosstalk, someone laughs)
[11:55] Ruth Gomez: pricing ask — can you give an estimated monthly for 200 qps, synthetic estimate?
[12:02] Avery Chen: we'll run a sample cost model after we see your average tokens per call. rough ballpark: Hosted fp16 at 200 qps might be X/month (we'll calc), fp8 will reduce that, Dedicated reserve gives a lower unit price but an upfront commit. we'll send concrete numbers.
[12:18] Diego Morales: ok jumping to the Evaluate tab — showing the top 10 regressions, sample diffs, and suggested fixes (tune qprofile, increase FP for KV cache).
[12:34] Samir Patel: can Optimize suggest prompt edits? sometimes small prompt changes fix hallucinations.
[12:40] Priya Kapoor: there is a suggestion engine that highlights prompt patterns correlated with regressions; it's not automatic rewrite but gives hints.
[12:48] Ruth Gomez: will we get alerts if a new canary introduces new hallucination types after rollout?
[12:52] Diego Morales: yes, continuous regression detection will flag new categories and can stop rollouts.
[13:04] (system note: meeting running over, summary time)
[13:12] Avery Chen: recap — action items: we'll provision sandbox, Diego will share baseline spreadsheet, Samir will upload 500 evals, Redwood will send compliance and pricing docs. next meeting: pilot kickoff prep on 2027-03-17.
[13:30] Ruth Gomez: sounds good. thanks, helpful walkthrough.
[13:36] Alina Park: appreciate the canary demo.
[13:40] (meeting ends)

Notes about transcription: speaker labels may be imperfect; short stutters like "um" and "ah" present; some proper nouns may be transcribed incorrectly (e.g., KMS/HSM as K-M-S).
